Recovery, uncertainty and the cost of waiting

A bounded recovery loop, equipment-specific duration beliefs, qualified retrieval planning and a faster preview path. The experiments below examine their limits as well as their outcomes.

What this changes

The release makes service recovery an observable, bounded process: completing work, confirming capacity and producing methane are separate outcomes. A repair receipt cannot stand in for a successful operating test. Conversely, useful degraded operation can resume before the observer has established full nameplate capacity.

The strongest qualification result is also a warning about policy stability. All null dispatch/state operands match exactly across modes and repeats. Outside the null case, the largest same-seed numerical-repeat difference is 115.55 kg of methane. In that risk-aware run, ambiguous observations at H15 reduced the capacity estimate from 450 to about 126.9 kW, below the 135 kW operating minimum. Verification expired overnight and the physically healthy electrolyser remained idle. There was no confirmed incident, so the zero false-alarm count does not describe this harmful uncertain derating.

Inspect the original hourly observations and estimates. This is a post-hoc counterexample, not an isolated causal test of risk preferences or the first point of numerical divergence.

The short recovery window exposes a consequential scheduling weakness. A repair near sunset can finish successfully, yet its verification window can expire before enough electricity is available for consecutive load tests. The controller then escalates rather than silently declaring recovery or endlessly renewing a deadline. This is a visible limit of the policy, not evidence that the physical repair failed.

The 24-hour sensitivity produces methane in six of nine cases, compared with none in the matched 12-hour damage cases; no case confirms full nameplate capacity. Its successful-output cases produce between 24.55 and 74.52 kg. The preselected seed-7 timeline remains unsuccessful and includes additional repair in the longer-window case. It is retained to show that a longer deadline is not sufficient by itself.

Service exposure also depends on the controller. Deferring uncertain cleaning can avoid energy, interruption and support costs, while leaving little new evidence about cleaning duration. The report therefore retains accepted work, actual activity, human visits and ending resources alongside production and costs. No mode is declared a general winner from these short cases.

In the main normal-service cases, the risk-aware arm has a mean assumed operating contribution of about €62, compared with about −€122 for the other modes. But it uses service fallback in 99 of 144 intervals and leaves mean modelled surface transmission at 80.54%, versus 85.02% for the other modes. Its apparent short-period cost advantage mixes avoided work, unresolved planning and a worse ending surface condition. It is not evidence of an optimal risk policy or a durable economic advantage.

The earlier broad run found a real model inconsistency: random job duration changed brush consumption without changing optical treatment at the same rate. The corrected release reconciles both against the same treated area. The original failed result remains failed and available in the programme history.

Where the evidence points next

  1. Fix the interaction between ambiguous observations and recovery scheduling. A single uncertain update can move the estimate below the minimum operating load and remove the next informative operating opportunity. Test uncertainty/covariance handling and deliberate re-observation around that boundary. Plan verification before committing work, accounting for daylight, stored energy, gas headroom and progressively larger load tests. Separate initial diagnosis from post-mission commissioning deadlines, retaining finite escalation and reporting useful production as well as full-capacity confirmation.
  2. Stabilise the comparison before expanding the controller family. Retain computation repeats and solver budgets alongside environmental seeds. Examine candidate truncation, service fallbacks and ending resources; then extend the most informative service exposures and time windows. A larger learned policy comparison would currently mix these effects with learning.
  3. Obtain identified operational observations. Repeated jobs on the same equipment are needed to distinguish persistent differences from job variation. Record unsuccessful and censored work, nominal recipes, weather/access conditions, support interruptions and observation availability. The new calibration interface can consume those data; synthetic fitting does not establish real distributions or repair capabilities.
  4. Extend contingent planning only with qualified branches. The implemented example permits charging after a nominated retrieval of an already observed stranded robot. Planning for a possible future interruption still needs explicit branches, observation boundaries, carrier/crew constraints and independent checks. It is not yet a general fleet-recovery planner.
  5. Bring first use under the latency budget. The repeated-interaction p95 is below 200 ms, including with batch activity, but cold interactions still exceed it. Isolate component initialisation and transport scheduling before adding prewarming or further caching, and measure the first interaction as its own acceptance condition.

These are follow-on steps, not a resumption of the separately paused fourteen-family hardware programme. The current evidence does not calibrate fault incidence, repair success, weather-error tails or annual return on service investment.

What the implementation now does

Repair → observed verification → escalation

A whole-mission return opens a distinct, finite verification window. Power, charging and load tests are planned together. Repeated observed shortfalls can support the existing bounded repair retry. Ambiguous or resource-blocked tests cannot certify a repair or justify an unlimited retry chain.

Original deadlines and failed episodes remain recorded. A later independent incident gets its own deadline. Disabling sensors does not mean recovered capacity.

Equipment effects and fresh job variation

Each asset and clock group has a posterior over declared persistent factors. Each accepted job gets a separate bounded multiplier. Its phases share that job factor. Completed clocks and right-censoring update the belief; candidate searches and rejected work consume no random draws.

The fixture's hidden persistent factor is 1.25, with fresh uniform job multipliers between 0.8 and 1.2. These are controlled assumptions, not measured fleet statistics.

Conditional return-to-charge planning

An observed stranded robot may be scheduled to charge after a qualified nominated retrieval and the complete crew return. Crew, carrier, route, work, energy and prices remain required. Retrieval grants no repair or readiness credit.

Future hypothetical interruptions retain conservative restrictions. The bounded example does not establish a general contingent fleet policy.

Coverage reconciles with consumables

The broader tests caught a missing coupling: fresh job duration changed brush consumption, while optical treatment still used the persistent factor alone. Coverage now follows the actual perform duration. Independent and runtime checks reconcile treated area with cleaning consumption.

Discarded allowance during brush replacement is recorded separately. Completed and 30%-interrupted passes are tested independently; no tolerance was relaxed.

Use the new loop in advanced experiment setup: shared visits and measured repair follow-up (service version 3), then bounded post-mission verification and escalation (recovery version 3). In Studies → uncertainty, choose Persistent equipment + job variation. These choices create new runs; archived decisions retain their original policies. Inspect a matched condition

Three service-uncertainty modes share plant parameters, economic objective, original prices, weather and event seeds. Null cases have two numerical repeats. Other main cases run for 48 hours with a 12-hour planning horizon. Process solves have a 0.25-second limit and service comparisons a two-second budget. The null process budget is two seconds.

This is a severe, controlled fixture: battery and hydrogen stores start empty. The persistent fault leaves 25% of 450 kW capacity (112.5 kW), below the 135 kW minimum operating load. The configured crew has zero response lead, 0.25-hour travel and 24-hour availability; robot batteries are 10 kWh, with three module kits initially available. These are shared illustrative assumptions chosen for service exposure, not measured site logistics or a typical fault distribution. Matching event seeds does not force identical realised repair outcomes: different accepted jobs or request times select different named draws. Finite solver budgets can also change those decisions.

The stock view includes robot energy, brush allowance and modelled surface transmission; remaining support-resource ledgers are in the saved summary and Study write-up. No terminal sale proceeds are assumed. The nine European windows use the first 48 UTC hours of cached ten-day ECMWF/ERA5 envelopes starting 10 January, April and July 2026 in London, Seville and Copenhagen. Original forecast publication boundaries are retained. ERA5 is reanalysis, not site measurement. No missing input is silently replaced.

Null traces identical across all modes and numerical repeats for every event seed: yes. Outside the null condition, finite-time solving can still change actions. Numerical repeats are not additional environmental seeds.

Same-condition computation variation

Across the repeated normal-service seed/mode pairs, the largest absolute methane difference was 115.55 kg; the median was 4.68 kg. These are observed differences between two executions, not confidence bounds or a general error guarantee.

Give verification another daylight opportunity

A separate sensitivity changes the recovery wait from 12 to 24 hours. Original service deadlines, physical parameters, prices and event seeds remain fixed. The setting governs both initial recovery tests and post-mission windows; this is a sensitivity to that shared policy parameter, not an isolated estimate of post-repair time. It does not guarantee that a procedure succeeds or that the observer will regain full-capacity confidence.

Follow the recovery clock

Fixed mode, seed 7, selected before the sensitivity completed. Change the deadline case and move through its original hourly record. Power is an interval average; capacity estimates are the information available at the decision boundary.

Grey power: actual PV. Amber power: delivered electrolyser load. Dashed pale power: requested load. In the lower plot, amber is estimated capacity and dashed grey is retrospective physical capacity. That physical trace was not available to the controller. Original operands and timing.

Physical restoration is retrospective simulator truth. Confirmation is an observed controller milestone. Confirmation here means an estimate at least 99.9% of nameplate capacity; useful degraded production can precede it. A scheduled test is only a prediction; missing confirmation is not replaced with a repair receipt. This sensitivity contains no additional null cases.

Calibrate predictions against observations

Calibration status: fitted. Three separate 240-hour Greedy observation runs exercise the workflow. Training uses packets available by H120; evaluation uses later new jobs, excluding continuations of training jobs. Candidate widths are predeclared, and held-out observations do not select the model.

The selected model has 172 held-out job/group outcomes. Its 90% predictive intervals covered 142 of 168 completed outcomes; 0 held-out jobs were outside the predictive support.

These are simulated observations. They verify fitting, causal holdout and prediction accounting. They do not establish empirical field calibration. Ten equipment/group histories remain sparse; four held-out outcomes are censored.

The finite persistent grid and uniform job distribution are model choices. Equipment-group fixture factors are held fixed within runs. Risk planning uses a small shared-quantile scenario approximation, not a fully calibrated joint distribution over independent future jobs.

The original checker rejected one calibration run after independent decimal replay put brush stock 0.000000000012539 m² below zero. That was the only failed check among 92,795. The revised checker expresses boundary violations in resource units and applies its existing numerical tolerance, with tests that reject material deficits and excesses. It does not clamp or change the physical trace. All three original records pass the new audit.

The original failed audit and two-run fit are preserved. This is a new calibration edition using the same predeclared candidate models and time cutoff. The calibration result identifies its physical source, checker, audit artifacts and fitting source separately. Checker correction and scope.

Responsiveness, including the cold tail

The preview path now passes the large immutable playback props as JSON scalars and decodes each update once. This avoids Gradio/Svelte repeatedly deep-snapshotting the complete run during loading-state changes. Numerical APIs and saved archives retain their structured values.
